blindSummary:
Trans visitors here face severe, state-directed risk. In 2024 the authorities escalated from hostility to active persecution: a culture-ministry decree reclassified transgender identity itself — the desire to live and be seen by others as a person of the opposite sex — as pornography, punishable by up to four years in prison. In September 2024 a wave of arrests targeted the community: the national LGBTQ+ organisation documented over 15 LGBTQ+ people detained, including at least eight transgender people, several arrested for merely subscribing to "extremist" resources online.

Detained trans people were beaten and forced to record humiliating "confession videos" circulated on pro-government channels. A regional security organisation's 2024 reporting notes that the majority of bias incidents here targeted trans people, including physical assaults, threats, abductions, humiliation, and coerced confessions related to their gender identity by law-enforcement officers. State media runs systematic dehumanising propaganda.

Gender transition technically remains legal, but the 2024 pornography decree means a discoverable online presence or simply living visibly as trans can be prosecuted. For a visitor: no documented trans-tourist case yet, but police actively hunt trans people, any visible gender nonconformity risks detention, and foreign nationals receive no protection.
blindOutOfScope: General political repression and the post-2020 protest crackdown affect everyone; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.

A legal news outlet (Sept 2024): the national LGBTQ+ organisation reported that 15+ LGBTQ individuals, including eight trans people, were detained within a month across several cities for allegedly subscribing to 'extremist resources'; most trans detainees were charged with hooliganism, two with pornography. Detainees reported physical and psychological abuse, and some fled the country. In February the prosecutor general had announced a bill to punish 'promotion of non-traditional relationships'.

Regional security organisation's 2024 hate-crime report on this country: the country has not reported hate-crime data to that body since 2015 and has no national point of contact; civil-society reports for 2024 came from a local human-rights NGO and others. No official data available.

A regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024), chapter on this country: state TV equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and described them as a tool of hostile foreign powers; the national LGBTQ+ organisation recorded increased hate speech in state propaganda; the prosecutor general's office plans an administrative-penalty law against 'LGBTI propaganda' (not yet tabled); at least ten trans people left the country in a year due to discrimination and repression; a new national security doctrine emphasises 'traditional values'.

An international LGBTI organisation's strategic-litigation case digest of UN treaty-body decisions (2024): compilation of decisions on 25 SOGIESC cases (criminalisation, asylum, violence, expression, families, legal gender recognition) - includes jurisprudence relevant to this country among other states.

A foreign government's archived 1999 human-rights report on this country: historical baseline - documents the legal and social situation including treatment of homosexuality under the long-standing president's government.

Academic legal report on equality before the law, written in an international human-rights organisation's 2006-2007 context: this country's constitutional equality guarantee versus reality - clampdown on civil society, harassment of activists, arbitrary detentions, death penalty retained; the legal and political climate facing LGBT people here.
